L2@P0: On the Traces of Operators
L3@P0: (from Grothendieck to Lidskii)
L4@P0: Didier Robert (Université de Nantes, France)
L5@P0: On the trace of operators
L6@P0: (from Grothendieck to Lidskii)
L7@P0: Didier Robert (Université de Nantes, France)
L8@P0: 1 Presentation
L9@P0: In this paper, the reader’s attention is drawn to some notions
L10@P0: that are classical in linear algebra but become more subtle to
L11@P0: deal with in the context of infinite-dimensional vector spaces
L12@P0: (endowed with a norm or a vector space topology). The Fredholm theory of integral equations, which will be mentioned
L13@P0: at the end of the article, shares many common points with
L14@P0: the systems of linear equations taught in the first year of undergraduate studies, except that the endomorphisms operate
L15@P0: on Banach spaces of the form C(K) (the space of continuous
L16@P0: functions on a compact K) or Lp(Ω) for a given measure on
L17@P0: Ω. In Fredholm theory, the notions of trace and determinant,
L18@P0: as well as their relations to eigenvalues, of course play the
L19@P0: same role as in finite dimension. Fredholm’s seminal article
L20@P0: “Sur une classe d’équations fonctionnelles” [Acta Mathematica, 27, pp. 365–390] goes back to 1903, a time when functional analysis was poorly developed. It was the starting point
L21@P0: of many works that partially motivated the advances in the
L22@P0: field throughout the 20th century (Hilbert, Banach, Fréchet,
L23@P0: Dieudonné, Schwartz, Grothendieck, Sobolev, Gelfand, Krein
L24@P0: and many others).
L25@P0: More recently, microlocal analysis and the theory of
L26@P0: pseudo-differential operators have allowed major progress in
L27@P0: understanding the non-self-adjoint operators that describe the
L28@P0: instability of certain systems in fluid or quantum mechanics.
L29@P0: Indeed, the location in the complex plane of the eigenvalues
L30@P0: with non-zero imaginary part enables one to get qualitative
L31@P0: information about the resonance of the system (see Zworski’s
L32@P0: paper [18] for an illustration of these phenomena). The recent
L33@P0: work [16] by Sjöstrand on Weyl formulas for randomly perturbed non-self-adjoint operators clearly shows the interest of
L34@P0: determinants in infinite dimension. By exploiting their subtle properties as entire functions on the complex plane, one
L35@P0: can obtain information about the eigenvalues. Lidskii’s trace
L36@P0: formula plays a pivotal role in these studies.

L243@P2: attribute the result to Lidskii. His original paper (1959), written in Russian, was translated in 1965, whereas [3] appeared
L244@P2: in 1963. Lidskii’s original proof was revisited and simplified
L245@P2: in [4]. The basic ideas will be explained at the end of this
L246@P2: article. The proofs mentioned above use the properties of determinants as entire functions of one complex variable. Other
L247@P2: proofs, more algebraic in nature, are based on the search for
L248@P2: triangular forms in infinite dimension [12].
L249@P2: In his monumental thesis, published in [5], Grothendieck
L250@P2: considerably developed the question of defining a trace (and
L251@P2: a determinant) for general classes of operators on Banach or
L252@P2: Fréchet spaces. He wrote his thèse d’État under the supervision of J. Dieudonné and L. Schwartz at Nancy University and
L253@P2: defended it in 1953. The reader is invited to look at the four
L254@P2: pages that L. Schwartz dedicates to A. Grothendieck in his
L255@P2: memoir book “A mathematician grappling with his century”
L256@P2: [pp. 282–286, Birkhäuser 2001]. Recall that Grothendieck received the Fields Medal in 1966 for his work in algebraic geometry.
L257@P2: One of the motivations of his doctoral research was to
L258@P2: establish a general setting for Fredholm theory, as an extension of the Schwartz kernel theorem [6]. Nevertheless, one
L259@P2: question seemed not to have been solved: when applied to
L260@P2: the particular case of Hilbert spaces, Grothendieck’s results
L261@P2: definitely give a proof of (5) but only for a more restrictive
L262@P2: class of operators than the natural trace class S1(H), namely
L263@P2: S2/3(H).
L264@P2: In [10, Section (27.4.11)], A. Pietsch obtained a sufficient
L265@P2: condition for equality (5) to hold in an arbitrary Banach space.
L266@P2: It contains the trace formulas of Grothendieck and Lidskii as
L267@P2: particular cases. Grothendieck’s approach to establish (5) for
L268@P2: Banach spaces is also discussed in [11].

L425@P3: 4 Traces and invariant functions
L426@P3: One can easily show that any invariant continuous linear form
L427@P3: f on S1(B) is a multiple of the trace Tr (see the introduction).
L428@P3: It is natural to look for other invariant functions on S1(B),
L429@P3: particularly for polynomial functions on other ideals of L(B).
L430@P3: Let us mention that Dixmier studied another property of
L431@P3: the trace: normality. Let L+(H) be the cone of positive operators on an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space H.
L432@P3: We call a trace any function f : L+(H) → [0, +∞] that is positive, additive and homogeneous. We say that f is a normal
L433@P3: trace if it is, moreover, completely additive: if A =
